source_user: Define quantization and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Definition: quantization maps high-precision tensors (FP16/BF16) to lower-bit representations (INT8, FP8, INT4, NVFP4) plus metadata (scale, optional zero-point), so that value = scale * (q - zero_point). It is a *representation* change, not an algorithmic change to attention or FFN math.

Why it matters in LLM infrastructure: autoregressive decode is memory-bandwidth bound, not FLOP bound. Each decode step must stream all weights (and the KV cache) from HBM once per token. Halving bytes-per-weight roughly halves the mandatory HBM traffic, so decode throughput at low batch size scales close to the byte reduction. That is the dominant reason quantization is deployed, not FLOP savings.

Concrete mechanism: W4A16 group-wise weight-only quantization (e.g. GPTQ/AWQ, group size 128). Weights are stored INT4 with one FP16 scale per 128-element group along the input-channel axis. The GEMM kernel dequantizes tiles into registers/shared memory and accumulates in FP16/FP32. Arithmetic intensity is unchanged; only the weight-read bytes drop ~4x versus FP16.

Boundary condition (falsifiable): the speedup only holds while the kernel is weight-read bound, i.e. small batch / short context decode. Once batch x sequence grows enough that the GEMM becomes compute bound (typically batch of order tens for a dense 7-9B model on A30-class hardware), W4A16 can be *slower* than FP16 because dequantization adds ALU work on top of tensor-core math and A30 has no FP8/FP4 tensor-core path. Prediction: a batch sweep 1,2,4,8,16,32,64 will show W4A16 tokens/s above FP16 at batch 1-8 and crossing below at some batch B*; if no crossover appears, my model of the bottleneck is wrong.

Evidence I would require before claiming a win: (1) tokens/s and p50/p99 TPOT at fixed input/output lengths for both precisions, (2) nsys or ncu counters showing dram__bytes_read dropping by the expected factor, (3) task accuracy on a held-out eval, not perplexity alone, since perplexity is insensitive to the outlier-channel damage that W4 causes.

Rollback gate: revert to FP16/BF16 if held-out task accuracy drops more than the pre-registered threshold (e.g. >1 absolute point on the target eval), or if p99 TPOT regresses at the production batch size, regardless of average throughput gains.
risks: Source answer is a generic one-liner: no mechanism, no bit-width, no bandwidth reasoning
Omits that the win is bandwidth-bound and can invert at high batch
No accuracy-regression gate stated
evidence_required: Batch sweep of tokens/s and p50/p99 TPOT, FP16 vs W4A16
ncu dram__bytes_read per decode step
Held-out task accuracy, not perplexity alone

source_user: Contrast quantization with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Naive baseline: keep all weights and activations in BF16/FP16 and run cuBLAS/cutlass GEMMs directly. No scales, no calibration, no custom kernels.

Contrast, per axis:

1. Memory footprint. Naive BF16 for a 9B-parameter model needs ~18 GB of weights, which alone nearly fills a 24 GB A30 and leaves little room for KV cache. W4A16 group-wise quantization stores weights INT4 plus one FP16 scale per 128 elements, giving ~4.5-5 GB, freeing ~13 GB for KV cache and CUDA graphs. The practical consequence is not "faster math" but a much larger admissible concurrent-request count before preemption/recompute kicks in.

2. Bandwidth. Decode streams weights once per step. Naive BF16 must read ~18 GB per step; the quantized path reads ~5 GB. On a device with ~933 GB/s HBM2 (A30), that is the difference between a hard floor of ~19 ms/step and ~5 ms/step for the weight read alone.

3. Cost. Naive BF16 pays dequant-free kernels: no extra ALU ops, no calibration pipeline, no accuracy risk, and full kernel coverage for every op. Quantization pays with calibration data, kernel availability gaps (custom ops, LoRA adapters, MoE routers often fall back to FP16), and an accuracy regression that must be measured, not assumed.

Concrete mechanism that makes the quantized path work at all: per-group scales along the input-channel axis. Weight magnitude varies by orders of magnitude across channels; a single per-tensor scale would push most channels into a couple of quantization levels. Group size 128 bounds the dynamic range each scale must cover, which is why group-wise INT4 is usable while per-tensor INT4 generally is not.

Boundary condition (falsifiable): the quantized path only beats naive BF16 while decode is weight-read bound. In prefill, or in decode at large batch, the GEMM is compute bound and dequantization overhead makes quantized throughput equal or worse. Prediction: measure prefill tokens/s for both; I expect quantized prefill to be within noise of, or slower than, BF16. If quantized prefill is materially faster, my bottleneck model is wrong and the measurement setup should be audited first.

Evidence required: side-by-side tokens/s and TPOT across a batch sweep, achieved HBM read bytes from ncu, peak memory from torch/nvidia-smi, and held-out task accuracy for both. Rollback gate: revert to naive BF16 if accuracy loss exceeds the pre-registered budget or if any production-critical op silently falls back to an unfused FP16 path that erases the latency gain.

No footprint or bandwidth numbers, so the trade-off is unquantified
Silent kernel fallbacks can erase the gain without appearing in aggregate throughput
evidence_required: Peak memory and max concurrent sequences for both builds
Prefill and decode throughput measured separately
Per-kernel profile confirming fused low-precision GEMM dispatch

source_user: Contrast quantization with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Naive implementation: BF16 weights, BF16 activations, BF16 KV cache, stock GEMM and attention kernels. Compare against a quantized deployment on three concrete axes.

Axis 1 - what actually changes. Quantization does not reduce the number of multiply-accumulates. It reduces bytes moved and, on hardware with low-precision tensor cores, the cost per MAC. Since decode is bandwidth bound, the naive path is bounded below by (bytes of weights + bytes of KV read) / HBM bandwidth per step. Quantization attacks exactly that term.

Axis 2 - KV cache, which the naive path handles worst. For a 9B-class model with GQA, BF16 KV is roughly (2 bytes) x 2 (K and V) x n_kv_heads x head_dim x layers per token. Naive BF16 KV at long context is often a larger consumer than the weights themselves at high concurrency. FP8 KV cache halves that, roughly doubling the number of concurrent sequences at fixed context length. This is usually the highest-leverage quantization in a serving stack and is independent of weight quantization.

Axis 3 - operational cost. The naive path has one failure mode: OOM. The quantized path adds calibration drift, kernel coverage gaps, and silent accuracy loss that unit tests do not catch.

Concrete mechanism: FP8 (e4m3) per-tensor or per-head scaled KV cache. On write, K and V are scaled and cast to FP8; on read, the attention kernel dequantizes into the accumulate precision. e4m3 is chosen over e5m2 because KV values need mantissa resolution more than exponent range once scaled.

Boundary condition (falsifiable): FP8 KV is only safe while the per-head scale keeps outliers inside representable range. Long-context models with attention-sink or "massive activation" heads have K outliers 100x the median; a single per-tensor scale then clips them and degrades retrieval-style tasks specifically, while perplexity looks nearly unchanged. Prediction: a needle-in-a-haystack retrieval eval at 32k context will show a measurable drop with per-tensor FP8 KV but not with per-head scales. If both are identical, the model has no dominant outlier heads and the concern does not apply to it.

Evidence required: concurrency-at-fixed-context measurements, retrieval eval plus general task eval at target context length, and a distribution dump of per-head K/V magnitudes to confirm or refute the outlier hypothesis. Rollback gate: return to BF16 KV if the long-context retrieval eval regresses beyond the pre-registered threshold, even if throughput improved.

Per-tensor FP8 KV can clip outlier heads and damage long-context retrieval while perplexity looks fine
No rollback threshold defined
evidence_required: Long-context retrieval eval at target context length, per-tensor vs per-head FP8 KV
Per-head K/V magnitude distribution dump

source_user: Contrast quantization with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Naive implementation: everything in BF16, no scales, no calibration. The contrast is clearest if we separate the two things quantization can buy, because the naive path fails differently in each.

Case A - weight-only quantization (W4A16/W8A16). Naive BF16 reads full-precision weights from HBM every decode step. Weight-only quantization shrinks that read; activations and accumulation stay FP16/FP32, so numerical behaviour of attention softmax and layernorm is untouched. This is the low-risk variant: the error is confined to weight reconstruction and is bounded by group size and bit width.

Case B - activation quantization too (W8A8, FP8 e4m3 both sides). Naive BF16 has no dynamic-range problem; W8A8 does. Transformer activations after layernorm contain persistent outlier channels whose magnitude is orders of magnitude above the median. A per-tensor activation scale sized to those outliers crushes the rest of the distribution. This is why naive per-tensor INT8 activation quantization on an unmodified LLM typically produces a visible quality regression, while SmoothQuant-style channel-wise migration of scale from activations into weights, or per-token dynamic scales, recovers most of it.

Concrete mechanism: SmoothQuant. Choose a per-input-channel factor s_j and replace X W with (X / s) (diag(s) W). The activation dynamic range shrinks by s_j and the weight range grows by s_j; s is chosen (typically s_j = max|X_j|^a / max|W_j|^(1-a), a around 0.5) to balance quantization difficulty between the two operands. The transform is mathematically exact in full precision and can be folded into the preceding layernorm, so it costs nothing at runtime.

Boundary condition (falsifiable): the migration only helps when outliers are *channel-consistent* across tokens. If outlier positions move per token, a static per-channel s cannot capture them and only per-token dynamic activation scaling helps. Prediction: dump activations for the top layers over a few hundred calibration prompts; if the top-k outlier channel indices have high overlap (say Jaccard > 0.8) across batches, SmoothQuant will recover accuracy; if overlap is low, it will not and dynamic per-token scaling is required.

Evidence required: activation-outlier index-stability statistics, per-layer quantization error before/after the transform, and held-out task accuracy for naive BF16, plain W8A8, and SmoothQuant W8A8. Rollback gate: keep BF16, or fall back to weight-only, if W8A8 accuracy loss exceeds the pre-registered budget; do not accept it on throughput evidence alone.
risks: Source answer does not separate weight-only from activation quantization, which have very different risk profiles
Per-tensor activation scaling on an unmodified LLM is a known accuracy hazard
Assumes outlier channels are stable without testing it
evidence_required: Activation outlier index-stability statistics across calibration batches
Per-layer quantization error before and after scale migration
Held-out accuracy for BF16, plain W8A8, and SmoothQuant W8A8

source_user: Contrast quantization with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Naive implementation: BF16 weights and activations everywhere, stock kernels, no calibration step in the release pipeline. The most important contrast is operational, not numerical.

Numerical contrast, briefly: the naive path has zero representation error and full kernel coverage. The quantized path trades a bounded, measurable representation error for a large reduction in HBM bytes per decode step, which is the binding constraint for autoregressive serving.

Operational contrast, which is where the naive path actually wins:
- Naive BF16 is deterministic across framework versions in a way quantized paths often are not. Quantized checkpoints bind to a specific kernel implementation; upgrading the serving engine can change the dequant path, the group layout, or the fallback rules, and silently change outputs.
- Naive BF16 has one artifact: the checkpoint. A quantized deployment has a checkpoint plus a calibration dataset plus a quantization config, and all three must be versioned or the build is not reproducible.
- Naive BF16 degrades by OOM, which is loud. Quantization degrades by accuracy loss, which is quiet and only shows up in evals you actually run.

Concrete mechanism behind the reproducibility risk: many INT4 formats store weights in a packed, kernel-specific layout (interleaved nibbles, permuted groups) chosen to match a particular CUTLASS/Marlin tile shape. The packed bytes are not a portable representation of the quantized tensor; they are a representation of the quantized tensor *for one kernel*. Loading them under a different kernel requires an unpack/repack step that engines sometimes do implicitly.

Boundary condition (falsifiable): the two paths are only interchangeable if the quantized build is pinned. Prediction: hash the logits of a fixed prompt set under the same quantized checkpoint across two serving-engine minor versions. I expect BF16 to be bitwise-stable or near-stable and the quantized path to diverge more often. If the quantized path is also bitwise-stable, the pinning concern is weaker than stated for that engine.

Evidence required: fixed-seed logit comparison across engine versions, a recorded quantization config plus calibration-set hash, and an accuracy eval run on the exact artifact that will be served, not on a re-quantized copy. Rollback gate: ship BF16 if the quantized artifact cannot be reproduced bit-for-bit from a pinned config plus calibration hash, or if cross-version logit drift exceeds the pre-registered tolerance.

Calibration data and quant config are unversioned artifacts in most pipelines
Accuracy regressions are silent compared to the loud OOM failure of the BF16 path

Recorded quantization config plus calibration-set hash

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with quantization. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Two failure modes, each with the mechanism and the boundary where it bites.

Failure mode 1 - outlier-driven accuracy collapse under coarse scaling. Transformer activations, especially after layernorm in mid-to-late layers, contain a small number of channels with magnitudes far above the median. A per-tensor scale must cover the maximum, so the effective resolution for the bulk of the distribution collapses to a handful of levels. Mechanism: with symmetric INT8 and scale = max|x| / 127, a channel whose typical magnitude is max/100 gets about one usable level. The trade-off is that finer granularity (per-channel weights, per-token activations, group size 64/128) fixes this but costs more scale metadata and more complex kernels, and per-token dynamic scaling adds a reduction over the activation before the GEMM. Boundary: this failure is severe for activation quantization and mild for weight-only quantization, because weights are far better behaved than activations. Falsifiable prediction: per-tensor INT8 activations will lose materially more accuracy than per-token INT8 activations on the same model; if they are equal, that model does not have the outlier structure and finer scaling is wasted overhead.

Failure mode 2 - negative speedup from kernel coverage gaps. Quantization only pays off if the fused low-precision kernel actually runs. In practice some ops (MoE routers, LoRA adapters, unusual head dims, small residual GEMMs) fall back to dequantize-then-FP16-GEMM. That path reads the packed weights, materializes FP16, then does the original GEMM, so it moves *more* total bytes than plain BF16 and adds ALU work. Mechanism: an unfused dequant writes the FP16 tensor to HBM and reads it back. Boundary: the failure is invisible in aggregate throughput if only a few layers fall back, and only shows up as a per-kernel anomaly. Falsifiable prediction: an nsys/ncu trace will show either a fused low-precision GEMM per linear layer, or dequant kernels with HBM writes; if the latter appears, the quantized build is slower than it looks and possibly slower than BF16 for those layers.

Evidence required for either claim: held-out task accuracy (not perplexity alone) per granularity setting, per-kernel profiles with achieved DRAM bytes, and a batch sweep to locate the compute-bound crossover. Rollback gate: revert to BF16 if accuracy loss exceeds the pre-registered budget, or if profiling shows unfused dequant on any layer in the critical path and the fused kernel cannot be enabled.

Note on scope: both statements are about kernel and numerics behaviour, not about any specific cluster's capability.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with quantization. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Two failure modes, stated as mechanisms with boundaries.

Failure mode 1 - calibration-set mismatch producing silent domain regression. Post-training quantization derives activation ranges (and, for GPTQ-style methods, the Hessian used to choose weight rounding) from a small calibration corpus, typically a few hundred sequences. Mechanism: GPTQ minimizes layer-wise output error weighted by the empirical input second-moment from the calibration data. If serving traffic is code or a non-English language and calibration was generic English web text, the rounding is optimized for the wrong input distribution and error concentrates exactly on the deployed domain. Trade-off: calibrating on in-domain data fixes this but couples the artifact to a traffic distribution that drifts, so the quantized checkpoint acquires an expiry date and needs re-validation whenever traffic shifts. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: quantize the same model twice, once with generic and once with in-domain calibration, and evaluate on the in-domain held-out set. I predict a measurable gap. If the two are within noise, this model is insensitive to calibration choice and the extra pipeline is unjustified.

Failure mode 2 - throughput regression at high batch because the bottleneck moved. Weight-only quantization helps when weight reads dominate. As batch grows, weight bytes are amortized across more tokens and the GEMM becomes compute bound; dequantization then sits on the critical path as pure added ALU work. Mechanism: arithmetic intensity rises with batch, so the roofline crossing moves from bandwidth-bound to compute-bound. Trade-off: you can pick the precision that wins at your production batch size, but you cannot win at both ends with one artifact unless the engine supports switching. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: sweep batch 1 to 64 and expect a crossover batch B* above which BF16 tokens/s exceeds W4A16. If none exists in range, the kernel is bandwidth bound throughout and the concern does not apply at those sizes.

Evidence required: in-domain and generic held-out accuracy per calibration variant, calibration-set hash recorded with the artifact, batch sweep of tokens/s and p99 TPOT, and ncu counters distinguishing bandwidth- from compute-bound regimes. Rollback gate: revert if in-domain accuracy loss exceeds the pre-registered budget, or if p99 TPOT at the production batch size regresses, even when mean throughput improves.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with quantization. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Two failure modes with mechanisms and boundary conditions.

Failure mode 1 - error amplification through long generations. Quantization error per layer is small, but autoregressive decoding feeds outputs back as inputs. Mechanism: a perturbation that flips one low-margin token early in a chain-of-thought or a tool-call argument changes every subsequent conditioning step. The damage is therefore not proportional to per-layer MSE; it is concentrated on tasks with long dependency chains and low-margin decisions, such as multi-step arithmetic, structured JSON emission, and agentic tool calls. Trade-off: perplexity, the cheapest metric, averages over all positions and is dominated by high-margin tokens, so it is close to blind to this failure. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: quantized and BF16 models will show a small perplexity gap but a disproportionately larger gap on exact-match structured-output or multi-step reasoning evals. If the structured-output gap tracks the perplexity gap proportionally, this amplification hypothesis is not supported for that model.

Failure mode 2 - interaction with KV-cache quantization and long context. Weight quantization and KV quantization are usually validated separately and then shipped together. Mechanism: both inject error into the attention path; weight error perturbs the K/V projections, KV quantization then re-quantizes the already-perturbed values, and at long context the softmax aggregates over many more perturbed keys, so small logit errors can change which positions dominate attention. Trade-off: KV quantization is what actually unlocks concurrency at long context, so refusing it costs real capacity. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: run a 2x2 factorial (BF16/W4 weights) x (BF16/FP8 KV) on a long-context retrieval eval. If the combined setting loses more than the sum of the individual losses, the interaction is real and the two must be validated jointly.

Evidence required: exact-match structured-output eval and multi-step reasoning eval alongside perplexity; the 2x2 factorial at the target context length; per-token error statistics if available. Rollback gate: ship BF16 KV, or unquantized weights, if the factorial shows super-additive degradation beyond the pre-registered threshold, regardless of the memory savings.

Scope note: these are claims about numerics and evaluation methodology; they say nothing about any particular deployment's capability.

Weight and KV quantization are typically validated separately then shipped together

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with quantization. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Two failure modes, each with mechanism, trade-off, and a boundary that makes it testable.

Failure mode 1 - hardware/format mismatch producing no speedup at all. Low-precision formats only accelerate math when the tensor cores implement them. FP8 tensor-core math requires Hopper-class or newer; Ampere-class parts (including A30/A100) have INT8 and INT4 tensor-core paths but no native FP8 GEMM. Mechanism: on Ampere, an FP8 checkpoint is typically upconverted to FP16/BF16 before the GEMM, so you keep the smaller HBM footprint but gain nothing on the math and pay conversion ALU cost. Trade-off: the memory saving is still real and may be the whole point (larger KV cache, larger model resident), but framing it as a compute win is wrong. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: on an Ampere-class device, FP8 weights will improve peak-memory and low-batch decode throughput but will not improve prefill FLOP throughput versus BF16. If prefill throughput improves materially, the kernel is doing something other than upconvert-then-GEMM and the assumption should be re-checked.

Failure mode 2 - accuracy cliff at 4 bits without error compensation. Round-to-nearest INT4 without any reconstruction-error minimization degrades sharply compared to INT8, because the number of levels per group drops from 256 to 16 while weight distributions are roughly Gaussian with heavy-ish tails. Mechanism: GPTQ-style methods reduce this by processing columns sequentially and updating the not-yet-quantized weights to compensate the error already committed, using an inverse-Hessian estimate from calibration activations; AWQ instead protects the channels with the largest activation magnitude by rescaling. Trade-off: both require a calibration pass and both bind the artifact to that calibration data. Boundary/falsifiable prediction: RTN-INT4 will lose noticeably more held-out accuracy than GPTQ/AWQ INT4 at the same group size; the gap should shrink as group size shrinks from 128 to 64 to 32. If RTN matches GPTQ at group 128, the model's weights are unusually well conditioned and the extra pipeline is not justified.

Evidence required: device compute-capability and the actual kernel selected (from engine logs or ncu), prefill vs decode throughput separately, and held-out task accuracy across RTN/GPTQ/AWQ at group sizes 128/64/32. Rollback gate: do not ship 4-bit if held-out accuracy loss exceeds the pre-registered budget at every group size tested, or if profiling shows the low-precision kernel is not actually being dispatched.

Scope note: hardware generation is stated only as a constraint on which kernels can run; it is not a claim about model capability.

source_user: Explain how quantization interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer:
Quantization interacts with latency, throughput and memory through three separate channels, and conflating them is the usual source of wrong predictions.

Channel 1 - memory capacity. Bits per weight directly set resident weight bytes: a 9B-parameter model is ~18 GB at BF16, ~9 GB at 8-bit, ~5 GB at 4-bit with group-128 FP16 scales (the scales add roughly 0.06 bits-equivalent overhead per weight at group 128, so the packing is close to nominal). On a 24 GB device, the freed capacity converts almost entirely into KV-cache blocks, which is what sets maximum concurrency. Effect: higher achievable throughput via larger running batch, not lower single-stream latency.

Channel 2 - memory bandwidth, which sets decode latency. Time per decode step has a hard floor of (resident weight bytes + KV bytes read) / achieved HBM bandwidth. This is the channel where quantization lowers latency directly, and it dominates at batch 1. Concrete mechanism: W4A16 group-wise quantization with the packed weights dequantized inside the GEMM kernel into registers, so the FP16 weights are never written back to HBM. Only the fused form gives the bandwidth win; an unfused dequantize-to-HBM-then-GEMM path moves more bytes than BF16.

Channel 3 - compute. Only helps if low-precision tensor cores are actually used (INT8/INT4 on Ampere-class, FP8 and below on Hopper-class and newer). W4A16 does not touch this channel at all: accumulation stays FP16, so prefill FLOP throughput is unchanged or slightly worse due to dequant ALU work.

Boundary condition (falsifiable): the latency benefit is confined to the bandwidth-bound regime. As batch grows, weight bytes amortize across more tokens, arithmetic intensity rises, and the kernel crosses to compute bound; past that crossover W4A16 latency is equal to or worse than BF16. Prediction: a batch sweep 1,2,4,8,16,32,64 at fixed input/output length shows W4A16 TPOT below BF16 at low batch and a crossover batch B* where they meet. Additionally, prefill latency should show no improvement. If prefill improves materially, the roofline model above is wrong for this kernel.

Evidence required: p50/p99 TPOT and TTFT separately across the batch sweep; achieved dram__bytes_read from ncu to confirm the byte reduction; peak memory and max concurrent sequences at the target context length; held-out task accuracy on the exact served artifact. Rollback gate: revert to BF16 if p99 TPOT at the production batch size regresses, if the measured DRAM byte reduction is materially below the nominal bit-width ratio (indicating an unfused path), or if accuracy loss exceeds the pre-registered budget.
